title: Multimode radiation pressure actuation of a mechanical resonator using a spatial mode sorter
authors: Morgan E. Choi, Daniel Allepuz-Requena, Diego Torres-Barajas, Neshat Sadafi, Dalziel J. Wilson
abstract: Multimode optomechanical scattering is ubiquitous in free-space imaging protocols, but its radiation pressure counterpart is challenging to detect with extended objects. Here we demonstrate radiation pressure actuation of a nanomechanical membrane using dynamically structured light from a spatial mode demultiplexer (SPADE). Using single- and two-mode illumination, we directly image the position-dependent intermodal coupling between Hermite-Gauss (HG) modes as mediated by the membrane's motion. As an application, we use multimode radiation pressure feedback to simultaneously cool two nearly degenerate membrane modes. Our results are applicable to diverse mechanical systems and serve as a stepping stone to SPADE-based quantum optomechanics.
summary: This research demonstrates how to use structured light from a spatial mode demultiplexer to exert a radiation pressure force on a mechanical membrane. By mapping the coupling coefficients, the authors show that two-mode illumination can probe spatial derivatives of the mechanical mode shapes. Crucially, they apply this to implement a feedback cooling scheme capable of simultaneously cooling multiple, nearly degenerate mechanical modes.
main_problem: The paper demonstrates the use of multimode radiation pressure to actuate and cool mechanical resonators, overcoming the difficulty of detecting radiation pressure effects with extended objects.
main_result: They successfully used two-mode structured light to map spatial derivatives of mechanical mode shapes and achieved selective, simultaneous cooling of two nearly degenerate mechanical modes.
method: The technique involves illuminating a nanomechanical membrane with structured light generated by a spatial mode demultiplexer (SPADE) to exert a radiation pressure force proportional to mode coupling coefficients.
model_or_system: The system is a $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ nanomechanical membrane resonator. The interaction is governed by the radiation pressure force, which depends on the coupling coefficients $ eta_{mn,kl}$ derived from the overlap of optical and mechanical mode profiles.
key_observables: Position-dependent intermodal coupling coefficients ($ eta_{mn,kl}$), mechanical mode shapes ($\varphi_{ij}$), and the raw displacement power spectral densities (PSDs) showing selective cooling.
important_parameters: The coupling coefficients $ eta_{mn,kl}$ are shown to be proportional to spatial derivatives of the mechanical mode shapes, allowing access to higher-order spatial information.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the reflected field approximation for the optical interaction, and the cooling process is modeled using a feedback force proportional to the mechanical velocity ($\propto -\dot{z}$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup, showing how single-mode and two-mode illumination maps reproduce squared or derivative forms of the mechanical mode shapes. A key figure shows raw PSDs demonstrating the selective and simultaneous cooling of two distinct mechanical modes.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework for multimode optomechanical scattering and radiation pressure force. It then details the experimental characterization of mode coupling using structured light. Finally, it applies this knowledge to implement a feedback cooling scheme to selectively cool multiple degenerate mechanical modes.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges quantum optics (structured light, mode coupling) with mechanical quantum systems (nanoresonators, cooling), providing a powerful, scalable tool for quantum state preparation in mechanical oscillators.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Multimode radiation pressure actuation of a membrane. A dynamically structured laser beam is produced by modulating the relative phase θ between two spatial modes u1 and u2 using a multi- plane light converter (MPLC). Reflecting the laser from a membrane (modeshape φ) results in a vibration amplitude z proportional to the optomechanical scattering coefficient β12 = ⟨u2|φ|u1⟩. Rastering the beam position (x0,y0) yields a radiation pressure map β12(x0,y0).

FIG. 2. Experimental setup and characterization of optical and mechanical modeshapes. (a) Experimental setup for two mode radiation pressure actuation and feedback control. PM = phase modulator. MPLC = Multi-plane light converter. f = lens for focusing onto membrane. XY = micropositioning stage for rastering location of beam on membrane. Green line = feedback of photocurrent from optical lever (purple). Inset: photograph of 2.5 mm square Si3N4 membrane. (b) Intensity profiles of single-mode umn and two-mode illumination fields u00 + αumneiθ produced by the MPLC, for |α|2 ≈0.1 and umn ∈{u00,u21,u11}. Red = model, orange = measurement. (c) Intensity profiles of membrane mechanical mode shapes...

FIG. 3. Single and two-mode radiation pressure maps for HG-mode illumination of a square membrane. Four mechanical modes φi j (rows) and illumination scenarios u00 +αumneiθ (columns) are shown, corresponding to radiation pressure maps β 2 00,kl(x,y). Blue (orange) = model (measurement): (a) Single-mode u00 maps β 2 00,00(x,y) from Fig. 2c. (b-d) Two-mode maps for umn ∈{u10,u01,u11} using α2 ≈0.1 (b,c) and 0.5 (d). Red dots in (b) and (c) show the beam position used for the feedback cooling data in Fig. 4.

FIG. 4. Mechanical-mode-selective feedback cooling via multi- mode radiaton pressure actuation. Raw displacement power spec- tral densities (PSDs) for near-degenerature φ21 and φ21 membrane modes are shown, overlaid with the normalized magnitude of the feedback controller gain: a 1-kHz-wide notch filter (light blue, right axis). Left (right) plot: selective cooling of the φ21 (φ12) mechani- cal mode via feedback to the relative phase of the u10 (u01) and u00 optical modes. Middle plot: simultanous cooling of φ21 and φ12 via feedback to both u10 and u01. The beam position on the membrane is indicated by a red circle in Fig. 3.
